### Question 1

Picture a fence at the top of a cliff and an ambulance parked at the bottom. Primary prevention is the fence: nothing has gone wrong yet, and the entire job is keeping it that way. Vaccines, helmets, and safe drinking water are all fences. The other three answers describe what happens after someone has already started to slip, has already landed, or is being treated more aggressively than their situation warrants.

### Question 2

Think about a tree damaged in a storm. You cannot un-break the branches, but you can brace the trunk, clean up the split wood, and help it keep growing. Tertiary prevention is the bracing. The disease has already happened, so the work shifts from stopping it to holding onto as much strength, mobility, and independence as the person can keep.

### Question 3

Secondary prevention works like a smoke detector. The fire has technically started, but it is small and you cannot see or smell it yet, and the alarm finds it in time to put it out. High blood pressure is exactly that kind of quiet fire: it damages arteries for years without symptoms, so measuring it and acting on the number counts as catching disease early, not as preventing it from starting.

### Question 4

Lay an illness out on a timeline: nothing wrong, then something quietly starting, then symptoms, then lasting damage. Primary prevention lives in the first stretch and secondary prevention lives in the second. The dividing line is where you are standing on that timeline, not who delivers the care or where it happens. That is why a nurse in a clinic and a lawmaker in a statehouse can both be doing primary prevention.

### Question 5

Compare a swimming lesson with rehabilitation after a shoulder injury. The lesson is for people who have never drowned, and its whole purpose is that they never will. The rehabilitation is for someone whose injury already happened, and its purpose is to get as much of that shoulder working again as possible. Both matter, but they serve completely different people, and that difference is exactly what separates primary from tertiary prevention.

### Question 6

Primary prevention is helping a teenager who already drinks four sodas a day cut back. Primordial prevention is shaping the town so soda never becomes the default: water fountains in every park, no soda ads at the ballfield, fresh food stocked in the corner store. One works on a habit that already exists; the other works on the world that keeps producing that habit in the first place.

### Question 7

Exercise does not come with a permanent label attached. Before you can name a level, you need two facts: which condition are we talking about, and does this person already have it? Walking to keep heart disease away is primary prevention. The same walking, at the same pace, as part of recovery after a heart attack is tertiary prevention. Same shoes, same street, different answer, because the label describes the person's situation rather than the activity.

### Question 8

Imagine a roof with a hole in it. Buying better mops and more buckets genuinely helps: the room becomes livable and the damage gets managed. But no amount of mopping patches the hole, so the water keeps arriving. Rehabilitation is the mop, and the tobacco policies and walking paths were the roof repair. Trade one for the other and you get a drier floor today alongside a leak that never stops.

### Question 9

Once the ulcer is open, the question is no longer whether this person will develop diabetes; that has already happened. The question is whether they keep the foot and keep walking. Tertiary prevention is that work. The disease and one of its complications are both present, so every effort goes toward stopping the damage from spreading and protecting the function that remains.

### Question 10

There are three ways to handle a loud factory: make the machines quiet enough that nobody's ears get hurt, test ears regularly to catch damage early, or help people once their hearing is already gone. Only the first one means no one's ears are ever harmed, and that is what makes it primary prevention. Safety experts also rank the ways to make a job safer: getting rid of the noisy machine is best, swapping in a quieter one is next best, then quieting the machine you already have, then rules like shorter shifts, and last of all earmuffs. Earmuffs are the weakest fix on that list, but they still stop damage before it starts — so being 'weaker' is not the same as being a different kind of prevention.

### Question 11

Before labeling anything primary, secondary, or tertiary, you have to finish the sentence: prevention of what? For blood pressure, the problem is already here and was caught quietly, so treating it is catch-it-early work. For stroke, nothing has happened yet, so the very same prescription is keep-it-from-starting work. One pill, two sentences, two labels, and both are right because they answer different questions.

### Question 12

Looking harder for a problem is not the same as stopping it. A metal detector sweeping a beach finds coins that were already dropped; it does not stop anyone from dropping them. Scanning healthy employees works the same way, which makes it finding rather than preventing. Sweeping everywhere also turns up harmless junk, which is why clinicians worry that testing without a reason leads to anxiety, biopsies, and procedures people never needed.
